name.text: Finding trigonometric ratios of negative angles using the unit circle

questiontext.text:
Draw the angle \(\theta = [[if test="is(unit=1)"]]{@theta@}[[else]]{@thetadeg@}^\circ[[/if]]\) in standard position. Start on the positive \(x\)-axis and, because \(\theta\) is negative, turn clockwise. The arm where you stop (the terminal side of \(\theta\)) meets the unit circle, the circle with centre \(O\) and radius \(1\), at a point \(P\). The diagram shows \(\theta\) and \(P\).

(a) Write down the coordinates of \(P\).

\(P = \Big(\) [[input:ansx]] \(,\) [[input:ansy]] \(\Big)\) [[validation:ansx]] [[validation:ansy]] [[feedback:prt1]]

(b) Find \(\sin\theta = \) [[input:ans_sin]] [[validation:ans_sin]] [[feedback:prt2]]

(c) Find \(\cos\theta = \) [[input:ans_cos]] [[validation:ans_cos]] [[feedback:prt3]]

(d) Find \(\tan\theta = \) [[input:ans_tan]] [[validation:ans_tan]] [[feedback:prt4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Worked Solution

A negative angle is measured clockwise from the positive \(x\)-axis. Wherever its terminal side meets the unit circle, that point is \(P = (\cos\theta,\, \sin\theta)\): the \(x\)-coordinate of \(P\) is \(\cos\theta\) and the \(y\)-coordinate is \(\sin\theta\).

(a) The coordinates of \(P\)

Step 1: locate \(P\). \(\theta = [[if test="is(unit=1)"]]{@theta@}[[else]]{@thetadeg@}^\circ[[/if]]\)[[if test="is(unit=1)"]], which is \({@thetadeg@}^\circ\)[[/if]], so we turn \({@a@}^\circ\) clockwise from the positive \(x\)-axis. That ends in the same place as turning \(360^\circ - {@a@}^\circ = {@pos@}^\circ\) anticlockwise, so \(P\) is in Quadrant {@qn@}.

Step 2: find the reference angle. The reference angle \(\alpha\) is the acute angle between \(OP\) and the \(x\)-axis (green in the diagram): [[if test="is(qP=1)"]]\(\alpha = {@pos@}^\circ\).[[/if]][[if test="is(qP=2)"]]\(\alpha = 180^\circ - {@pos@}^\circ = {@refang@}^\circ\).[[/if]][[if test="is(qP=3)"]]\(\alpha = {@pos@}^\circ - 180^\circ = {@refang@}^\circ\).[[/if]][[if test="is(qP=4)"]]\(\alpha = 360^\circ - {@pos@}^\circ = {@refang@}^\circ\).[[/if]]

Step 3: find the sizes of the coordinates. In the right-angled triangle with hypotenuse \(OP = 1\), the horizontal side is \(\cos {@refang@}^\circ = {@cref@}\) and the vertical side is \(\sin {@refang@}^\circ = {@sref@}\).

Step 4: give each coordinate its sign. In Quadrant {@qn@}, \(P\) is [[if test="is(qP=1 or qP=4)"]]to the right of the \(y\)-axis, so \(x\) is positive,[[else]]to the left of the \(y\)-axis, so \(x\) is negative,[[/if]] and [[if test="is(qP=1 or qP=2)"]]above the \(x\)-axis, so \(y\) is positive.[[else]]below the \(x\)-axis, so \(y\) is negative.[[/if]] Therefore

\[ P = \left( {@x_coord@},\; {@y_coord@} \right). \]

(b) \(\sin\theta\) is the \(y\)-coordinate of \(P\): \(\sin\theta = {@sin_theta@}\).

(c) \(\cos\theta\) is the \(x\)-coordinate of \(P\): \(\cos\theta = {@cos_theta@}\).

(d) \(\tan\theta\)

\[ \tan\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{ {@sin_theta@} }{ {@cos_theta@} } = {@tan_theta@}. \]

[[if test="is(qP=1 or qP=3)"]]\(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\) have the same sign, so \(\tan\theta\) is positive.[[else]]\(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\) have opposite signs, so \(\tan\theta\) is negative.[[/if]]

Check with the identities for negative angles. \(\sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta\), \(\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta\) and \(\tan(-\theta) = -\tan\theta\). For example, \(\sin({@thetadeg@}^\circ) = -\sin {@a@}^\circ\) and \(\cos({@thetadeg@}^\circ) = \cos {@a@}^\circ\), which give the same values.

prtcorrect.text: Correct answer, well done.

prtpartiallycorrect.text: Your answer is partially correct.

prtincorrect.text: Incorrect answer.

truefeedback.text: That is the point for \(+\theta\): you have turned anticlockwise. \(\theta\) is negative, so turn clockwise from the positive \(x\)-axis. This changes the sign of the \(y\)-coordinate.
Your \(y\)-coordinate is right, but your \(x\)-coordinate has the wrong sign. Look at the diagram: is \(P\) to the left or to the right of the \(y\)-axis?
Both of your signs are wrong, so your point is in the quadrant opposite to \(P\). Look at where \(P\) is in the diagram, then decide the sign of each coordinate.
It looks as if you have swapped the coordinates. The \(x\)-coordinate of \(P\) is \(\cos\theta\) and the \(y\)-coordinate is \(\sin\theta\).

falsefeedback.text: Find the reference angle (the acute angle between \(OP\) and the \(x\)-axis) and use its exact cosine and sine for the sizes of the coordinates. Then use the quadrant of \(P\) to give each one its sign.

truefeedback.text: The size of your answer is right, but the sign is wrong. Remember \(\sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta\): turning clockwise changes the sign of the \(y\)-coordinate. Is \(P\) above or below the \(x\)-axis?
Your answer has the size of \(\cos\theta\). \(\sin\theta\) is the \(y\)-coordinate of \(P\), not the \(x\)-coordinate.

falsefeedback.text: \(\sin\theta\) is the \(y\)-coordinate of \(P\). Use your answer to part (a).

truefeedback.text: The size of your answer is right, but the sign is wrong. Remember \(\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta\): turning clockwise does not change the sign of the \(x\)-coordinate. Is \(P\) to the left or to the right of the \(y\)-axis?
Your answer has the size of \(\sin\theta\). \(\cos\theta\) is the \(x\)-coordinate of \(P\), not the \(y\)-coordinate.

falsefeedback.text: \(\cos\theta\) is the \(x\)-coordinate of \(P\). Use your answer to part (a).

truefeedback.text: The size of your answer is right, but the sign is wrong. Remember \(\tan(-\theta) = -\tan\theta\). Check the signs of \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\) before you divide.
It looks as if you have divided the wrong way round. \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\).

falsefeedback.text: Use \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\) with your answers to parts (b) and (c).
